title: Houthi Strikes Hit Saudi Aramco Facilities at Jizan and Yanbu as Red Sea Oil Route Comes Under Threat
excerpt: Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis attacked critical Saudi oil infrastructure along the Red Sea coast, sending shipping traffic to its lowest level in months.
body:
• Yemen's Houthis struck Saudi Aramco facilities in Jizan and Yanbu over the weekend, targeting the kingdom's Red Sea oil export route that bypasses the blockaded Strait of Hormuz.
  • Video verified by Reuters showed a large column of smoke rising from the Aramco refinery in Jizan, which has a capacity of 400,000 barrels per day.
  • Two ballistic missiles aimed at Yanbu oil installations were intercepted by a U.S.-made Patriot battery operated by Greece under an agreement with Riyadh.
  • Ship traffic through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait fell to 11 commodity vessels on Sunday, the lowest level in months.

The Attacks

Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group struck sites belonging to Saudi Aramco in Jizan and Yanbu on Saturday, describing the operation as retaliation for what he called Saudi drone incursions into Yemeni airspace. Video shared on social media and verified by Reuters showed a large column of smoke rising from the direction of the Aramco refinery in Jizan.

Two Asia-based trading sources told Reuters they had been informed of potential damage to fuel and oil storage sites at Jizan. The refinery there has a capacity of 400,000 barrels per day. In Yanbu, two ballistic missiles aimed at oil installations were intercepted by a U.S.-made Patriot battery operated by Greek military personnel under an agreement with Riyadh, according to Greek security sources.

Why Yanbu Matters

Yanbu has become Saudi Arabia's most critical oil export hub since Iran blockaded the Strait of Hormuz after the U.S.-Israeli attacks in February. The kingdom rerouted crude output to Yanbu via its east-west pipeline, making the Red Sea port the primary exit for Saudi oil shipments.

The Houthis declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia last week, with Houthi leader Abdul Malik al-Houthi saying all Saudi oil facilities could be targets. The threat has opened a second front in the disruption to global oil supplies, which had already been choked by the Hormuz blockade.

Shipping Grinds Down

Ship traffic through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait fell to just 11 commodity vessels on Sunday, the lowest level in months, according to shipping data from Kpler. Physical crude cargo prices in the Middle East, Europe and Africa jumped to two-month highs last week.

Among the few vessels still transiting, four exited the Red Sea on Sunday, including a Hong Kong-flagged supertanker carrying two million barrels of Saudi crude for eastern China. A separate tanker carried 750,000 barrels of Saudi crude for Pakistan.

Oil Price Whiplash

Brent crude surged above $100 a barrel last week for the first time since May before plunging below $92 on Monday after Trump paused U.S. strikes on Iran. WTI crude fell more than 7 percent as investors reduced the geopolitical risk premium. But analysts warn the reprieve may be short-lived.

"Houthi attacks on Saudi Aramco infrastructure at the critical port of Yanbu threaten to starve energy-poor Asia of vital crude oil flows."

— Benjamin Picton, Senior Macro Strategist, Rabobank

Saudi Arabia has responded with airstrikes on Houthi military facilities in Yemen's Hodeidah port and has mobilised the Saudi-backed Yemeni government's air force against Houthi positions. Both sides in Yemen's civil war — paused under a ceasefire since 2022 — are now mobilising forces along the front, with the Houthis effectively joining the broader conflict alongside their Iranian allies.
